I would pretend to die. My pleased heirs would take my fortune, and in exchange I would gain freedom. But I had to plan carefully. I could not leave myself penniless; I must put some money aside. What disgusting tricks I was being driven to! Yet the alternative was a whole lifetime of lies. Whenever guilt over planning a deception made me hesitate, a visit from some aunt or cousin would drive me back to the scheme and strengthen my resolve. They would tell me that everyone must die. Then they would suggest that my father had certainly lost his mind after my mother’s death. They said he was mad and that I was lucky, since in one of his fits he might have killed me instead of destroying himself. Of course, they expressed all this delicately, avoiding plain words that might hurt my feelings.

They whispered their meaning through dark hints, softly and quietly.

They lowered their eyes and offered sympathetic smiles or sighs. I listened with a calm face while every nerve shook, not daring to say yes or no to these terrible insults. What a delightful life, so entirely free of deceit! I wore a dove’s innocent expression and carried a fox’s heart. I felt only the shame of lying, without any comforting sense of innocence to redeem it. Once I had dressed myself in the bright clothing of honesty; now I must borrow a costume of many colors. It might fit awkwardly at first, but practice would teach me to arrange it elegantly, to lie gracefully. Yes, I might stain my soul with falsehood until its original color disappeared. Beloved father, accept your unhappy daughter’s pure heart! Let me join you as unspoiled as before, or you will not recognize what I have become. As grief might change Constance, deceit would change me, until in heaven you would say, “This is not my child.” Father, to find happiness now and when we meet again, I must escape this life, which is a mockery to someone like me. Only in solitude can I be myself. Only in solitude can I be yours.

Even now I look back with disgust at the schemes and tricks through which, after many painful struggles, I finally escaped. I could describe at length how I first secured a small income for the rest of my life, and then made certain that everyone believed me dead. I could tell all this, but I will not.

“But in the vicious attack on Chantilly published in yesterday’s ‘Musée,’ the satirist made some disgraceful references to the shoemaker’s change of name when he became an actor, and quoted a Latin line that you and I have often discussed. I mean this line:

“‘Perdidit antiquum litera prima sonum.’

“I explained that it referred to Orion, which used to be spelled Urion. Certain pointed details connected with that explanation convinced me you would remember it. Clearly, then, you were bound to connect Orion with Chantilly. The particular smile that crossed your lips told me you had done so. You were thinking of the poor shoemaker’s humiliation. Until then you had been walking with a stoop, but now I saw you straighten to your full height. That convinced me you were considering Chantilly’s small stature. At that moment I broke into your thoughts to observe that, since Chantilly was in fact such a little fellow, he would be better suited to the Théâtre des Variétés.”

Not long afterward, we were reading an evening edition of the “Gazette des Tribunaux” when the following paragraphs caught our attention.

“Extraordinary Murders.—At about three o’clock this morning, residents of the Quartier St. Roch were woken by a series of dreadful screams. They apparently came from the fourth floor of a house in the Rue Morgue known to be occupied only by Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, Mademoiselle Camille L’Espanaye. After unsuccessfully trying for some time to gain entry in the usual way, eight or ten neighbors forced the entrance gate with a crowbar and went inside with two police officers. By then the screaming had stopped. As the group rushed up the first flight of stairs, however, they heard two or more harsh voices arguing angrily, apparently in the upper part of the house. On reaching the second landing, they found that these sounds too had stopped, leaving complete silence. They separated and hurried from room to room. Eventually they reached a large back bedroom on the fourth floor. Its door was locked, with the key on the inside, so they forced it open. The sight that greeted them horrified everyone present as much as it astonished them.

“The room was in utter chaos, with furniture smashed and scattered in every direction. There was just one bed frame; its mattress had been pulled off and thrown into the middle of the floor. A blood-smeared razor lay on a chair.

Her face changed color, and she fell silent.

Mrs. Gardiner stood a little behind her. When Elizabeth paused, he asked whether she would do him the honor of introducing him to her friends. She was completely unprepared for this courtesy and could barely keep from smiling. He was now seeking an introduction to some of the very people whose connections had offended his pride when he proposed to her. “How surprised he will be,” she thought, “when he learns who they are! At the moment he thinks they belong to fashionable society.”

Nevertheless, she introduced them immediately. As she explained their relationship to her, she stole a glance at him to see his reaction, half expecting him to retreat as quickly as possible from such embarrassing company. He was plainly surprised by the connection, but bore it bravely. Instead of leaving, he turned to walk back with them and began talking to Mr. Gardiner. Elizabeth could not help feeling pleased and triumphant. It was reassuring that he should discover she had relatives she had no reason to be ashamed of. She listened closely to their entire conversation, delighting in every phrase and sentence from her uncle that revealed his intelligence, taste, or good manners.

Their conversation soon turned to fishing. She heard Mr. Darcy invite her uncle, with the greatest politeness, to fish there whenever he wished during his stay in the neighborhood. He also offered him fishing equipment and pointed out the stretches of stream where the fishing was usually best. Walking arm in arm with Elizabeth, Mrs. Gardiner gave her a look of astonishment. Elizabeth said nothing, but felt immensely pleased. Surely this courtesy was entirely for her benefit. Yet her amazement was profound, and she kept asking herself, “Why has he changed so much? What could explain it? It cannot be because of me; he cannot have softened his manners for my sake. My accusations at Hunsford could not have produced such a change. He cannot possibly still love me.”

They walked for some time like this, the two women ahead and the two men behind. After going down to the riverbank to examine an unusual water plant more closely, they resumed walking in a slightly different arrangement. Mrs. Gardiner caused the change: tired from the morning’s exercise, she found Elizabeth’s arm insufficient support and chose her husband’s instead.
